ENT Clinical Note – Telemedicine Visit  

Subjective:
- Presenting complaint and possible trigger/exposure  
  • Intermittent severe frontal headaches, sense of “feeling hot,” palpitations, episodic shortness of breath, bilateral arm tingling, reduced appetite, 5-lb unintentional weight loss, decreased libido.  
  • Symptoms began after changing jobs; occur primarily while at work (computer use, meetings) where stress rated 7–8/10.

- Symptom timeline and progression  
  • New over the past several weeks–months (exact start not specified).  
  • Headaches and autonomic symptoms occur separately, not always simultaneous; frequency variable (palpitations ~ once daily).  

- ENT-related symptoms  
  • Throat swelling/closure sensation: None reported.  
  • Voice change/hoarseness: None.  
  • Dysphagia/odynophagia or drooling: None.  
  • Nasal/ocular symptoms: None.  
  • Stridor/noisy breathing: None.  
  • Dyspnea: Episodic shortness of breath while seated at desk; not with exercise.  
  • Swelling (lips/tongue/uvula/face): None.  
  • Ear pain/hearing change: None.  
  • Neck pain/swelling: None.

- Relevant past episodes/treatments  
  • No prior similar episodes; no prior ED visits, epinephrine use, or airway interventions mentioned.

- Allergies and current medications  
  • Allergies: “None” stated.  
  • Medications: Thyroxine – dose/route/frequency not documented.

- Social context  
  • 35-year-old lawyer working in London; high occupational stress; alcohol ~2 glasses wine/week; non-smoker; no recreational drug use.  
  • Call conducted in a private setting; no other person present noted.

Objective:
- Observable swelling/distribution: None stated.  
- Airway/breathing: No stridor; patient reports episodic SOB but normal exercise tolerance.  
- Mental status: Alert, coherent; reports stress but no syncope/dizziness described.  
- Vitals & physical examination: Not recorded (tele-visit).  
- Companion: None mentioned.

Assessment:
Suspected endocrine or stress-related etiology for new headaches and autonomic symptoms; no evidence of acute ENT airway compromise.

Evidence summary  
• On thyroxine therapy with heat intolerance, palpitations, weight loss → possible biochemical hyperthyroidism.  
• Symptoms cluster at workplace during high stress → supports anxiety/panic or tension headache component.  
• No ENT red-flag airway findings (no throat swelling, voice change, stridor).

DDx (aligned with transcript)
1. Iatrogenic hyperthyroidism from excessive thyroxine replacement – heat intolerance, weight loss, palpitations, and decreased libido; needs TFTs.  
   Opposing: No tremor/diarrhea; symptoms fluctuate with work stress.  
2. Stress-related anxiety/panic disorder with tension-type headaches – temporal link to job change and workplace stress; explains palpitations, SOB, tingling.  
   Opposing: Objective weight loss and heat intolerance less typical.  
3. Primary tension or migraine headaches – frontal severe headaches with mild nausea precipitated by screen time; does not explain systemic symptoms fully.

Plan:
- Schedule prompt in-person clinic visit for full physical examination including cardiovascular and respiratory assessment.  
- Order blood tests: thyroid function (TSH, free T4/T3), complete blood count, electrolytes, glucose, B12 if neurologic symptoms persist.  
- Discuss ergonomics, hydration, and stress-reduction strategies pending evaluation.  
- Advise patient to seek urgent care (call 999/EMS) if sudden worsening shortness of breath, chest pain, persistent palpitations, neurological deficits, or any throat swelling/voice change develops.  
- Provide information on booking appointment via clinic app; clinician to forward visit summary to in-person provider.  
- Follow-up: Review results and symptom progression within one week of labs or sooner if red-flag symptoms arise. Consider ENT or neurology referral only if new airway or focal neurologic findings emerge.

Quality checks (document_quality):
● Missing expected elements: vital signs, in-office ENT/airway examination, thyroxine dose & compliance details, exact symptom onset date, formal allergy list confirmation, auto-injector/previous anaphylaxis plan (not applicable but routinely assessed in ENT airway notes).  
● Conflicts between transcript and DDx: Patient states past “hyperthyroidism” yet is taking thyroxine (replacement) – etiology unclear (conflict noted).  
● Transcript quality: Generally clear; occasional clipped/overlapping speech but key clinical details intelligible.
